claims.text: A refractory high-entropy alloy containing only low-activation elements can serve as a structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors.
Tungsten, tantalum, chromium, and vanadium are examples of low-activation elements suitable for the proposed alloy.
The as-cast refractory HEA has high-temperature strength.
The as-cast refractory HEA has inherent irradiation resistance due to its multi-element composition.
Eliminating elements that produce long-lived radioactive species under neutron irradiation will reduce long-lived activation products.
High-temperature thermomechanical processing will enhance the alloy's microstructural stability.
The proposed HEA has a stable multiphase microstructure.
Refractory elements strengthen the grain boundaries of the proposed HEA.
The cocktail effect in high-entropy alloys provides phase stability.
The cocktail effect in high-entropy alloys enhances irradiation resistance.
Selecting low-activation elements minimizes the production of long-lived radioactive byproducts.
Phase stability, irradiation resistance, and reduced activation will help maintain the alloy's mechanical integrity after irradiation.
The modified refractory HEA will have superior high-temperature mechanical properties compared with conventional plasma-facing-component materials under fusion-reactor conditions.
The modified refractory HEA will have lower residual radioactivity than conventional plasma-facing-component materials under fusion-reactor conditions.
Conventional fusion plasma-facing-component materials tend to accumulate activation products.
Conventional fusion plasma-facing-component materials tend to degrade under high thermal and irradiation stresses.
Unexpected phase formation may impair the performance of the proposed alloy.
